verdicts.why: A remote point in time is named plainly; choosing 'distance' over 'far-off time' says nothing about the speaker's attitude.
The interval between two times is a measure, and the word takes no side on it.
'It escaped my notice' states that something was not experienced, with no judgement of the thing or the person.
Fleeing implies something to flee from, but that is the meaning, not an attitude toward the fleer or the thing fled; 'escape' against 'leave' adds urgency, not approval or contempt.
Getting away for pleasure or diversion is described, not praised or sneered at.
Gas or steam that escapes simply issues from an opening; a physical description with no stance.
Breaking off an activity is stated as a fact; any rudeness belongs to the act, not to the word, which is used as readily of arrivals and events as of people.
A clear mental image is named without approval or dismissal of what is pictured.
A print or slide of a person or scene is a plain object name.
Calling a film 'a picture' is dated register, not a judgement of the film.
'The picture of health' intensifies a quality that the following noun supplies; the word itself carries no attitude of its own.
'The overall picture' treats a situation as something to be viewed and says nothing about whether it is good or bad.
Illustrations in a text are named plainly, neither praised nor belittled.
The visible part of a television signal is a technical description.
A topic under consideration is being discussed; the word describes the process without judging its object.
A fee paid to retain services is a legal term with no attitude attached.
A variation from the norm is stated as a fact; unlike 'deviance' or 'aberration', 'difference' does not disapprove of it.
The result of a subtraction is an arithmetic term with no stance.
An unverified explanation is named neutrally; the word neither endorses nor doubts it the way 'speculation' or 'theory' might colour it.
'Immediate relief' or 'immediate assistance' locates something in the present moment; strong in meaning but not an attitude.
Having no intervening medium is a plain structural description.
Electrical or acoustic noise that disturbs a signal is a technical term; the disturbance is the referent, not a judgement, and the meddling sense that does judge is not this gloss.
The football term names a play, legal or penalised by rule, without the speaker taking a side.
A narrative account of past events is described plainly; 'tell such a story' can imply a fib in context, but that comes from the sentence, not from this sense of the word.
A news item is named neutrally, as against 'puff piece' or 'exposé' which would judge it.
